true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate `downsize` definition shadows 4-arg version

app/models/optimized_image.rb defines self.downsize twice: once as (from,to,max_width,max_height,opts) and again as (from,to,dimensions,opts). In Ruby the second definition overwrites the first, so any existing caller using the 4-argument max_width/max_height form will now raise ArgumentError (wrong number of arguments). This silently breaks backward compatibility while adding the new 3-argument form used for percentage downsizing.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client validation hardcodes 10MB and ignores type setting

validateUploadedFile replaced Discourse.SiteSettings['max_'+type+'_size_kb'] with hardcoded 10*1024. This ignores both max_image_size_kb and max_attachment_size_kb and breaks admins who raise limits above 10MB (client rejects files server would accept) or lower attachment limits below 10MB (client allows files server will reject). Keep per-type site-setting lookup; if large images are to be downsized server-side the image limit needs explicit handling, not a global hardcode.

true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Animated downsize passes percentage to gifsicle resize-fit

OptimizedImage.downsize_instructions_animated just delegates to resize_instructions_animated, which builds gifsicle --resize-fit <dimensions>. The new upload flow passes "80%" as dimensions. gifsicle expects WxH for --resize-fit, not a percentage, so animated GIF downsizing will fail, return false, and large GIFs will never be reduced to SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.

true_positives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Loop checks tempfile.size instead of path size, never sees shrink

In UploadsController#create_upload the retry loop checks tempfile.size while OptimizedImage.downsize overwrites tempfile.path in place via an external convert process. tempfile.size stats the open file descriptor, which still points to the old inode if the converter unlinks/recreates the path, so the size appears unchanged. The loop then always runs all 5 iterations and shrinks an image to ~0.8^5 (~33%) even when one pass would have sufficed. Use File.size(tempfile.path) to stat the path.

false_positives.candidate:
413 error message hardcodes 10MB

displayErrorForUpload for HTTP 413 replaced Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb with hardcoded 10*1024. The alerted max_size_kb will be wrong whenever the configured limit differs from 10MB, and it always reports the image limit even for attachment uploads. Read the message value from site settings.

In-place downsize with unchecked return risks data loss

UploadsController calls OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, ...) using the same file as source and destination and never checks the return value. If convert/gifsicle fails it can truncate or corrupt the only copy of the upload, and the code retries the same failing command up to 5 times then proceeds to create the Upload from the corrupted/oversized file. Use a separate temp destination and abort/handle error if downsize returns false.

Remote download hardcodes 10MB ignoring site settings

FileHelper.download for API-provided URLs was changed from SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes to a hardcoded 10.megabytes. Admins who configured a larger max_image_size_kb will have valid remote images rejected/truncated at 10MB, and the limit no longer tracks configuration. The cap should derive from site settings, e.g. max of image/attachment limits.

false_positives.candidate:
Email unsubscribe link requires login, fails logged-out

In app/controllers/topics_controller.rb unsubscribe is behind before_filter :ensure_logged_in with no email token, while the link post.topic.unsubscribe_url is sent in notification emails. A recipient opening the email in a logged-out browser, different device, or email client is redirected to login and the unsubscribe never executes, making the advertised per-topic unsubscribe unusable. Needs a signed one-click token like DigestUnsubscribeKey or explicit login-then-confirm flow.

State-changing unsubscribe on GET

In app/controllers/topics_controller.rb TopicsController#unsubscribe mutates notification_level and calls tu.save! inside a GET action wired in config/routes.rb as get t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe. GETs are prefetched by email scanners, browsers, crawlers and are not CSRF-protected, so merely opening/scanning the email or link can silently change subscription state. State change must be POST/PUT/DELETE with CSRF/form token, or at minimum require confirmation.

Either always mute or fix copy to explain two clicks are required.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Validation has DB write side effect, double-counts every signup

lib/validators/email_validator.rb calls BlockedEmail.should_block?(value) from validate_each, and should_block? increments match_count and updates last_match_at with save. UsersController#create calls user.valid? and then user.save, which validates again, so one signup attempt increments match_count twice and touches last_match_at twice. Any other valid?/invalid paths also mutate stats even when the user is never saved, making match_count/last_match_at unreliable for abuse monitoring.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive, allowing trivial bypass

app/models/blocked_email.rb does BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first with the raw submitted value and neither BlockedEmail nor User downcases/normalizes email before this check. PostgreSQL string equality is case-sensitive, so if an admin blocks bad@spammers.org an attacker can register BAD@spammers.org or Bad@Spammers.org, miss the block list, pass EmailValidator, and create the account. The block feature is therefore defeatable by changing case.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

false_positives.candidate:
Non-atomic read-modify-write on match_count loses updates

app/models/blocked_email.rb implements stats as record.match_count += 1; record.last_match_at = ...; record.save. Under two concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked email both threads read the same count, increment locally, and save, so one increment is lost. It also runs full validations/callbacks and touches updated_at for a stats counter. Use an atomic increment such as increment_counter/update_counters/update_all instead.

Wrong Ember dependent key means rejected email never shows invalid

app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js declares emailValidation as .property('accountEmail', 'rejectedEmails.@each') but rejectedEmails is an array of plain strings. @each only observes properties on array members, not array membership, so pushObject in createAccount does not invalidate emailValidation. After the server rejects a blocked email the field keeps showing OK until the user edits the email text, defeating the purpose of the rejectedEmails cache.

Fix by using escape_javascript / to_json for the origin and by passing only the origin (scheme://host:port), not the full URL.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

false_positives.candidate:
EmbedController spec contradicts implementation

The spec expects EmbedController#best to call TopicRetriever.new(...).retrieve when no embed exists, but the implementation enqueues Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic,...) and renders loading. The test will fail and does not cover the actual async path, the 1.minute expiry, or visibility of the TopicView. Fix the spec to expect the job enqueue.

Invalid X-Frame-Options ALLOWALL breaks embedding

EmbedController sets response.headers['X-Frame-Options'] = "ALLOWALL". ALLOWALL is not a defined directive. Browsers treat unknown values as DENY/SAMEORIGIN and will refuse to frame the content, defeating the embed feature. To allow framing the header must be removed, not set to ALLOWALL.

Non-atomic throttle key can leak permanently

TopicRetriever#retrieved_recently? does $redis.setnx(key,1) then $redis.expire(key,60) as two separate commands. If the process crashes between them the key never expires and that embed_url is throttled forever. It also creates one unbounded key per distinct URL. Fix by using a single atomic SETEX / SET NX EX.

SSRF and unhandled fetch in import_remote

TopicEmbed.import_remote calls open(url).read on a URL that ultimately derives from the embed_url query param via Jobs::RetrieveTopic -> TopicRetriever -> fetch_http. There is no timeout, size limit, error handling, or redirect restriction. TopicRetriever only checks the initial host equals embeddable_host, but open-uri follows redirects to any host and ignores ports, allowing port-scanning / internal network access and causing job exceptions / hangs when the remote site is down.

content_sha1 updated even if revision fails

In TopicEmbed.import the update path calls revisor.revise! then unconditionally does embed.update_column(:content_sha1, content_sha1). If revise! returns false or the post is nil/deleted, the hash is still advanced, so the new content is lost and will never be retried because future imports compare equal. Fix by only updating the hash on successful revision and handling missing embed.post.

raw_html cook path stores unsanitized HTML leading to stored XSS

Post#cook returns raw verbatim when cook_method is raw_html, skipping the entire rendering/sanitization pipeline. TopicEmbed.import sets cook_method to raw_html for RSS/readability content and app/views/embed/best.html.erb renders it with <%= raw post.cooked %>. Any <script>, on* handler, iframe or form in the feed or scraped article is stored and later served to all embed viewers. Fix by sanitizing on import or on cook.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fallback lookup hits SiteSetting on every translation without normalization

FallbackLocaleList#[] in config/initializers/i18n.rb is called by the I18n fallbacks backend on every translated key and executes [locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq.compact. That means every I18n.t does a SiteSetting read plus allocation. With hundreds of translations per page this is significant overhead. It also never normalizes the incoming locale to a symbol, so a string 'en' and symbol :en are not deduped by uniq, producing duplicate chain entries, and string entries never match the symbol entries in @loaded_locales, causing repeated load_path scans.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

false_positives.candidate:
Translate only loads current locale, can cache missing translation

I18n.translate in lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb only calls load_locale(config.locale) before delegating to the backend, but the new fallback chain is [user locale, SiteSetting.default_locale, :en]. If the fallback locale files are not yet loaded the backend lookup misses and returns 'translation missing'. That result is stored in the global LRU cache. Any code path that did not run ApplicationController#set_locale (Sidekiq jobs, mailers, console, standalone backend calls) can therefore poison the cache, and later web requests that did preload fallbacks will still hit the cached missing string until LRU eviction or reload!.

Translation cache key ignores fallback chain

The LRU key in lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb is built only from key plus config.locale plus backend object_id. The rendered value now depends also on SiteSetting.default_locale, which is part of the fallback chain. Changing the site default locale or updating a fallback-locale translation does not invalidate existing entries, so users whose own locale misses will keep seeing the old fallback string until the entry is evicted, reload! is called, or the process restarts.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Passkeys conditional UI now requires a known user, disabling it on initial login

isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) returns webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled() && user != null. It is used in authenticate() and challenge() to decide whether to call webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context). Previously the code filled the form when passkeys were enabled and context.getUser() == null (initial login). Now it only fills when context.getUser() != null (re-authentication). The PR's own tests still expect //form[@id='webauth'] on the first page.

false_positives.candidate:

createErrorResponse() calls context.form().setError(...), context.form().setAttribute(...), AuthenticatorUtils.setup...(context) which uses another context.form(), fillContextForm(context) whose returned LoginFormsProvider with new challenge and attributes is discarded, then return errorChallenge.apply(context) which builds yet another fresh form. Because each context.form() is a new instance, the error, ENABLE_WEBAUTHN_CONDITIONAL_UI flag, and the fresh challenge/attributes never make it into the returned Response. On passkey failure the user gets a page without the error displayed and without valid conditional-UI data, and the auth-session challenge note does not match what was rendered.

The caller in AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator.badPasswordHandler() and WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator.createErrorResponse() then creates a different instance via challenge()/errorChallenge.apply() which internally calls context.form() again. Each context.form() returns a new LoginFormsProvider, so attributes set on the first instance never reach the rendered response. After a failed password/passkey during re-authentication the page will show the regular login with editable username and registration link instead of hidden-username re-authentication.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative queryset slice crashes instead of paginating

In src/sentry/api/paginator.py OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result allows start_offset=cursor.offset when enable_advanced_features and offset<0, then does queryset[start_offset:stop]. Django QuerySets explicitly reject negative indexing with AssertionError/ValueError, they do not wrap like Python lists. The comment claiming Django handles negative slicing automatically is false. Consequence: an attacker-controlled cursor string like value:-10:0 reaches an unhandled exception and returns 500, a remotely triggerable availability issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator breaks datetime ordering

In src/sentry/api/paginator.py OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does math.floor/ceil directly on getattr(item, self.key) and value_from_cursor returns cursor.value as int. The only caller in src/sentry/api/endpoints/organization_auditlogs.py uses order_by="-datetime", so the key is a datetime object. math.floor(datetime) raises TypeError and filtering a datetime column against int 0 in build_queryset is a type mismatch. Consequence: any request with optimized_pagination=true crashes with 500 or paginates incorrectly instead of behaving like DateTimePaginator.

false_negatives.golden_comment: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.
Importing non-existent OptimizedCursorPaginator

false_positives.candidate:
Global BasePaginator offset clamp is inconsistent and wrong

In src/sentry/api/paginator.py BasePaginator.get_result was changed for all APIs from queryset[offset:offset+limit+extra] to start_offset=max(0,offset) for forward cursors but keeps raw offset for is_prev cursors and for the later check len(results)==offset+limit+extra. Other paginators in the same file (OffsetPaginator, ChainPaginator, CombinedQuerysetPaginator) reject offset<0 with BadPaginationError (400). Consequence: this global change silently coerces invalid forward cursors to page 0 instead of 400, still crashes for is_prev negative offsets, and miscomputes has_more when clamping because the length check uses the unclamped offset.

New paginator and endpoint branch have no tests

In src/sentry/api/paginator.py a new OptimizedCursorPaginator class and a modified BasePaginator path plus a new optimized_pagination branch in OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint were added with no unit or API tests. Consequence: the datetime-key crash, negative-slice crash, and paginate-kwarg mismatch above are uncaught, and future changes to global pagination have no regression coverage.

Unknown paginate kwarg enable_advanced_features

In src/sentry/api/endpoints/organization_auditlogs.py the optimized branch calls self.paginate(..., paginator_cls=OptimizedCursorPaginator, enable_advanced_features=True). Base endpoint paginate does not define that parameter and does not forward arbitrary kwargs to the paginator constructor in the established codebase. Consequence: the optimized path either raises TypeError for unexpected keyword argument returning 500, or silently drops the flag so the paginator never actually enables the intended mode, making the branch dead/broken.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator allows negative-offset DB slicing

In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features is true and cursor.offset < 0, the code sets start_offset = cursor.offset (negative) and slices queryset[start_offset:stop]. Django QuerySets do not support negative slicing and raise AssertionError, so a crafted cursor string like "0:-5:0" causes a 500/DoS. The comment claiming Django handles negative slicing automatically is false, and other paginators in the same file explicitly reject offset < 0 with BadPaginationError.

true_positives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BasePaginator now passes negative offset for prev cursors

BasePaginator.get_result was changed from queryset[offset:stop] to start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset. For is_prev cursors the offset is used unclamped, so a client-supplied cursor with negative offset and is_prev=1 still reaches queryset[negative:stop]. This is inconsistent with OffsetPaginator/ChainPaginator which reject negative offsets, and causes AssertionError or undefined paging.

false_negatives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.

false_positives.candidate:
Hidden optimized_pagination flag switches to vulnerable paginator

The endpoint adds an undocumented ?optimized_pagination=true query param that, for any superuser or member with has_global_access, switches from DateTimePaginator to OptimizedCursorPaginator with enable_advanced_features=True. This exposes the negative-offset path to a broad set of users on a sensitive audit-log endpoint with no tests or validation, widening attack surface unrelated to the spans-buffer title.

Mandatory end_timestamp_precise lookup crashes consumer on missing field

process_batch now does val["end_timestamp_precise"] with direct dict access. Any span event missing that field raises KeyError inside the Arroyo batch, failing the whole batch, blocking commits and causing consumer crash-loop/backlog instead of skipping or defaulting. Previously Span did not require the field.

Redirect traversal cut from 10000 to 1000 fragments deep traces

The redirect-following loop was reduced from 10000 to 1000 iterations. Traces/segment trees deeper than 1000 will stop early with an unresolved set_span_id, so spans that should merge into one segment stay in separate Redis keys and flush as fragmented segments. This is a correctness regression for deep traces to save Lua time.

ZUNIONSTORE without AGGREGATE MAX corrupts scores on duplicates

The migration from SUNIONSTORE to ZUNIONSTORE uses default SUM aggregation. If the same payload member exists in both source sets (retry, duplicate ingest, overlapping parent/span buffers), its score (end_timestamp_precise) is summed to 2x timestamp, corrupting ordering and future ZPOPMIN eviction victims. Should use AGGREGATE MAX.

max_segment_spans enforcement removed, truncation is silent

_load_segment_data no longer checks max_segment_spans, drops the segment_span_count_exceeded metric and error log, and leaves max_segment_spans config unused. Oversized segments are now silently truncated to 1000 in Lua via ZPOPMIN (hardcoded, off-by-one vs 1001 default) and flushed as incomplete instead of being skipped/logged, causing silent span loss.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unstable hash() cache key with 60s stale allowlist returns wrong counts

In src/sentry/api/helpers/error_upsampling.py the cache key is built with Python hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids))). Python hash() is salted per-process, so different workers produce different keys and never share cache, and collisions are possible. Worse, the cached value is only allowlist eligibility cached for 60 seconds. If the allowlist changes, queries for up to 60s use the stale decision and return upsampled sum(sample_weight) instead of count() or vice versa. invalidate_upsampling_cache is defined but never called anywhere, so there is no invalidation. The new endpoint tests reuse the same org and project ids with different mocked allowlists, so the second test will hit the first test's cached True and get wrong results.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling check uses outer dataset and request instead of scoped query

In src/sentry/api/endpoints/organization_events_stats.py _get_event_stats receives scoped_dataset and query as arguments but calls is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request) using the outer closure dataset and the original request. The dashboard-split factory calls the same function with split_dataset=discover and rewritten queries like (query) AND !event.type:transaction. Because the check ignores scoped_dataset and the query argument and instead inspects request.GET, split queries are evaluated against the wrong dataset and wrong query string, so errors routed to discover will not be upsampled and transactions routed elsewhere may be.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

false_positives.candidate:
Error detection only matches event.type:error substring

In src/sentry/api/helpers/error_upsampling.py _is_error_focused_query returns True only if the lowercased request query string contains event.type:error. It misses the queries this endpoint itself generates for the discover split, e.g. (query) AND !event.type:transaction, misses empty or default discover queries that include errors, and misses event.type:default/error variants. It also false-positives on substring matches like message:event.type:error. Consequence is discover error traffic silently uses raw count() instead of upsampled_count() or vice versa, producing inconsistent charts.

Test helper silently overwrites sample_rate with unvalidated value

In src/sentry/testutils/factories.py _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling wraps all access in bare try/except pass, checks if client_sample_rate truthy, then does float(client_sample_rate) with another swallowed exception and unconditionally assigns normalized_data[sample_rate]. It does not validate 0 < rate <= 1, so 0, negative, >1, or string values either silently pass or silently fail, and it overwrites any legitimate existing sample_rate. This creates invalid test fixtures that do not represent production validation and can mask missing server-side checks.

Transform only handles bare count() and discards original alias

In src/sentry/api/helpers/error_upsampling.py transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling only rewrites columns where lowered stripped value equals count(), always emitting upsampled_count() as count. It drops any original alias like COUNT() as my_count, does not handle yAxis forms with aliases, equations, or count_if/count_unique, and leaves other count-like aggregates unconverted. Consequence is broken aliases for top-events/orderby that expect the original name and dashboards mixing upsampled and raw counts in the same response.

upsampled_count assumes sample_weight exists and truncates with toInt64

In src/sentry/search/events/datasets/discover.py upsampled_count is defined as toInt64(sum(sample_weight)) with no coalesce, ifNotFinite, or null handling. The helper comments admit it assumes sample_weight exists for all events in allowlisted projects. Older events, non-sampled events, or transactions in a mixed discover query will have NULL/missing sample_weight, so sum can be NULL/0 and counts collapse to 0. toInt64 also truncates fractional weights like 1/0.3=3.33, systematically undercounting. The result is wrong chart values instead of falling back to count().

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).

Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.

Backup-code login can bypass password check

File packages/core/EventManager.ts declares `credential` once outside the `for (const reference of calendarReference)` loop and then assigns `credential = this.calendarCredentials.filter(...)[0]` inside. If a later reference's credential is not found in memory and not found in DB, `credential` is not reset to undefined and still holds the previous iteration's credential. The code then calls `updateEvent(credential, ...)` with the wrong user's credential, updating the wrong calendar or crashing on undefined on the first iteration.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Minimum token schema uses invalid computed keys

File packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts defines minimumTokenResponseSchema with computed keys [z.string().toString()]. That evaluates to a literal property name like the stringified Zod object, not a catch-all. The schema does not mean access_token plus any expiry field; it requires a nonsense property. Use z.object({access_token: z.string()}).passthrough() or catchall instead. As written sync-mode validation will reject valid provider responses or accept wrong shapes.

true_positives.golden_comment: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Non-atomic retryCount increment loses retries

In scheduleSMSReminders.ts both failure paths do data: {retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1} using the value read at the start of the cron run. If two cron invocations overlap or the same reminder is processed concurrently, both read the same value and write back the same increment, losing one retry. The reminder can then never reach the >1 threshold and be retried forever. Use atomic Prisma update data: {retryCount: {increment: 1}} instead of read-modify-write.

The comment and intent is SMS-only cleanup. This causes data loss for other channels if they ever use retryCount and can delete future scheduled reminders. Org-scope expectation assumes deterministic DB row order

The org-scope test at packages/lib/server/service/__tests__/insightsBooking.integration-test.ts:333 expects teamIds = [org.id, team.id, team2.id, team3.id] and userIds = [user.id, user2.id, user3.id] in that exact order. Database return order is undefined, so the ANY(...) arrays can come back in any order. The test will flake or fail when Postgres returns rows in a different order even though authorization is correct. The test must sort both expected and actual arrays or assert order-insensitively.

Public findMany method deleted without migration

packages/lib/server/service/insightsBooking.ts previously exposed findMany(findManyArgs) that applied authorization and filter conditions via a Prisma where clause. This PR deletes that method and only exposes getBaseConditions() returning Prisma.Sql for manual $queryRaw use. Deleting a public service method in the same change that converts internals to raw SQL is a breaking contract change and requires updating all call sites in the same PR.

toEqual on Prisma.Sql compares template segmentation, not SQL semantics

The test at packages/lib/server/service/__tests__/insightsBooking.integration-test.ts:295 expects team/org/combined conditions with expect(conditions).toEqual(Prisma.sql`...flat template...`). The service builds the same SQL text via nested interpolation, e.g. Prisma.sql`(${acc}) OR (${condition})` and Prisma.sql`(${acc}) AND (${condition})` in buildOrgAuthorizationCondition, buildTeamAuthorizationCondition and buildFilterConditions. Prisma.Sql stores strings[] plus values[]; nested Sql values are flattened by splicing, so the resulting strings[] segmentation differs from a hand-written flat template even when the final SQL text and bound values are identical. toEqual therefore fails on false negatives, making the authorization/filter tests red while the query is semantically correct. Tests should compare rendered SQL plus values or execute the query instead of deep-equaling Sql objects.

This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Async reminder cancellations fired without await

updatedBookings.forEach calls deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder, both async functions doing Prisma updates and SendGrid/Twilio calls, without awaiting or collecting promises. true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete cancels SendGrid but never deletes DB row

deleteScheduledEmailReminder with immediateDelete=true (used for reschedule in handleNewBooking.ts and for workflow/step delete in workflows.tsx) POSTs batch cancel to SendGrid and then returns without deleting or updating the workflowReminder row. The row stays with scheduled=true and the old referenceId. For reschedule there is no cascade delete, so orphan rows accumulate, are never marked cancelled for the cron to pick up, and past-date cleanup is the only eventual removal. false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
Cancel query too broad and past-cancelled rows deleted without SendGrid cancel

remindersToCancel filters only on cancelled:true and scheduledDate, with no method=EMAIL, scheduled=true, or referenceId-not-null filter, so it can attempt SendGrid cancel with batch_id null and fail the whole batch. Worse, the earlier deleteMany at line 34 deletes all EMAIL reminders with scheduledDate in the past, including cancelled ones, without calling SendGrid. Those rows disappear from the cancel query so their scheduled sends are never cancelled. Filter the cancel query and run cancels before blind past-date deletes.

One SendGrid failure aborts all pending email cancellations

The cron wraps the entire for-loop of SendGrid cancel calls and the Prisma deletes in a single try/catch. If client.request throws for any one reminder, the loop aborts, remaining reminders are never attempted, and the workflowRemindersToDelete array built so far is never awaited because Promise.all is skipped on exception. One bad batch_id therefore leaves all other cancelled emails scheduled and they will still be sent. Handle each reminder independently.

Paid bookings return before workflow reminders are cancelled

When booking.paid is true the handler refunds, updates status to REJECTED, awaits apiDeletes and returns at line 464. The workflow-reminder cancellation loop at lines 485-493 is below that return and never runs for this path. Paid cancelled bookings therefore keep their scheduled email/SMS workflowReminders and the reminders are still sent. Move reminder cancellation before the paid early-return or duplicate it there.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Recurring cancel deletions never awaited

In handleCancelBooking.ts the code iterates calendar credentials with `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); ... apiDeletes.push(await calendar?.deleteEvent(...)) })`. A `forEach` with an async callback is fire-and-forget; the outer function does not await the callbacks. Later the code does `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))`, but at that point `apiDeletes` has not yet been populated by the still-pending callbacks. Consequence: for recurring cancellations with `allRemainingBookings`, calendar deletions are lost or race with the response, leaving stale events on external calendars and incorrect availability.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully

false_positives.candidate:
Async forEach leaves calendar/video deletes unawaited

Consequence: deletion errors are silently lost as unhandled rejections and reschedule can report success while external calendar/video events remain.

Async forEach leaves calendar/video deletes unawaited

In wipemycalother/lib/reschedule.ts the code does `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...); return deleteMeeting(...) })` inside a `try` block. `forEach` does not await async callbacks, so the `try/catch` cannot catch asynchronous rejections and the function proceeds to send email and `return true` immediately. Consequence: deletion errors are silently lost as unhandled rejections and reschedule can report success while external calendar/video events remain.

Reschedule deletions fire-and-forget via async forEach

In bookings.tsx `requestReschedule` does `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { if (...) { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...); } else ... return deleteMeeting(...) })` with no await on the loop and no `Promise.all`. The returned promises from `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` are also not awaited or collected. Consequence: the handler sends the reschedule email and webhooks before old calendar/video events are deleted, failures become unhandled rejections, and old time slots may never be freed, causing double-bookings.

getCalendarCredentials now returns promises in sync API

In CalendarManager.ts `getCalendarCredentials` is still a synchronous function but now does `const calendar = getCalendar(credential)` where `getCalendar` is async and returns `Promise<Calendar|null>`. The returned objects therefore contain `calendar: Promise` instead of `Calendar|null`. Only `getConnectedCalendars` was updated to `await item.calendar`. Any other consumer of this exported function expecting a truthy calendar instance or calling calendar methods directly will get a Promise object (always truthy) and fail. The contract change is invisible in the sync signature and breaks callers and type expectations.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours end check ignores event length

In checkIfIsAvailable both `start` and `end` are computed as `slotStartTime.hour()*60+slotStartTime.minute()`. `end` never adds `eventLength`. A slot that starts inside working hours but ends after `workingHour.endTime` (e.g. 60-min event starting 30 min before close) passes the check and is reported available, allowing bookings that overflow availability.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dayjs objects compared with === never equal

In checkIfIsAvailable the code tests `dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...)` to detect a zero-length date override (day marked unavailable). `dayjs()` returns an object, so `===` compares object identity and is always false. As a result a full-day block is never detected, `dateOverrideExist` stays true and the function later returns true (available). A day the host blocked off will still show bookable slots and can be booked.

false_positives.candidate:
Date-override containment misses slots overflowing the override

In checkIfIsAvailable a slot is deemed outside a date override only if `slotEnd <= overrideStart` or `slotStart > overrideEnd`. A slot that starts inside the override but ends after `override.end` (e.g. override 10:00-11:00, slot 10:30-11:30) satisfies neither condition, so `find` returns undefined and the slot is treated as inside the override and returned as available. This allows bookings that extend beyond the override window. The same block also uses `isAfter` instead of same-or-after for the end boundary, so a slot starting exactly at override end is treated as inside.

Date-override timezone shift drops day rollover

In getSlots an override is converted to invitee minutes-since-midnight via `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset).hour()*60+minute`. Only hour/minute are kept and the result is applied to the original `startOfInviteeDay`. If the invitee-organizer offset moves the override across midnight, the portion belonging to the adjacent invitee day is still placed on the original day (or `start >= end` and skipped entirely). This creates slots on the wrong day or drops availability for timezones far apart.

Timezone offset computed from Date.toString()

In getSlots the offsets are computed as `dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone)` and `.tz(timeZone)`. `Date.toString()` produces a locale-dependent string without explicit offset that dayjs must re-parse, which can lose the original instant, depend on server locale, and give the wrong `utcOffset()` around DST. The Date object should be passed directly to dayjs, e.g. `dayjs(override.start).tz(...)`, to preserve the instant.

Working-hours check fails with split hours

In checkIfIsAvailable availability is rejected if `workingHours.find(workingHour => slot is outside that workingHour)` finds any entry. If a user has two intervals on the same weekday (e.g. morning and afternoon), a slot inside one interval is outside the other, so `find` always succeeds and every slot is marked unavailable. The correct test is that a slot is available if it is inside any interval, not that it is outside any interval. Fixed hosts with split hours will show no slots.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError crash when Integration metadata has no sender

In src/sentry/integrations/github/integration.py GitHubInstallation.dispatch does pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") != integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]. If the Integration was created before sender tracking, via the normal pipeline without a webhook, or metadata lacks sender, this raises KeyError/TypeError resulting in a 500 instead of the intended github-integration-failed.html error page. It is a denial-of-service and breaks reinstall of legacy integrations.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing
OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

false_positives.candidate:
Fresh installs skip GitHub-user ownership check

In src/sentry/integrations/github/integration.py GitHubInstallation.dispatch returns pipeline.next_step() immediately when Integration.DoesNotExist for the supplied installation_id, without comparing github_authenticated_user to the installer. The sender comparison on lines 501-505 only runs when an Integration row already exists (e.g. created by webhook). A fresh installation_id with no row yet therefore creates an Integration without proving the Sentry user is the GitHub user who installed the app, defeating the PR's stated mismatch protection and depending on a webhook race.

Unhandled token-exchange / user-info failures give 500 not error page

In src/sentry/integrations/github/integration.py OAuthLoginView.dispatch calls safe_urlopen for the OAuth access_token exchange and get_user_info(payload["access_token"]) without try/except. Only the missing-access_token and missing-login cases are handled.

installation-not-found 404 path no longer tested

In tests/sentry/integrations/github/test_integration.py test_installation_not_found stubs a 404 for /app/installations/{id} but then drives the new OAuthLoginView with code/state ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05 that mismatches pipeline.signature, so it asserts b"Invalid installation request." from the state check and never exercises build_integration's 404 handling ("The GitHub installation could not be found."). The 404 branch is now uncovered.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
queued default evaluated once at import time

In src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py the field is declared as `queued: datetime = timezone.now()`. The call to timezone.now() runs once when the module is imported, so every AssignmentSource created without an explicit queued value shares the same timestamp. It should be `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`. Consequence: provenance timestamps are wrong and any future debounce / ordering logic based on queued will be broken.

true_positives.golden_comment: to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
to_dict/from_dict datetime does not survive task queue round-trip

AssignmentSource.to_dict() in src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py uses dataclasses.asdict, which leaves `queued` as a datetime object. src/sentry/integrations/utils/sync.py puts that dict into `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async` kwargs, which must be JSON serializable for Celery. After JSON round-trip the value comes back as a string, and AssignmentSource.from_dict() does `cls(**input_dict)` with no parsing, so `queued` becomes a str violating the declared datetime type. Consequence: task enqueue can fail or produce type-confused objects; serialization should use isoformat and parse back.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.

false_positives.candidate:
Missing coverage for allow-other-integration and deassign blocking

In tests/sentry/models/test_groupassignee.py the only cycle test is test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration which asserts outbound is suppressed when source equals target. There is no test that a different source integration still syncs outward, nor that deassign with a matching AssignmentSource is suppressed. Consequence: a regression that over-suppresses all outbound sync or that leaves the deassign loop unfixed would not be caught.

Same-integration check does not stop multi-integration ping-pong

In src/sentry/integrations/mixins/issues.py should_sync() returns False only when `sync_source.integration_id == self.org_integration.integration_id`. src/sentry/integrations/utils/sync.py fans outbound assignee sync out to every GroupLink for the group. If one Sentry group is linked to two different integrations A and B, an inbound assign from A is blocked from echoing to A but still syncs to B, B's webhook then re-enters as inbound from B and syncs to A, forming an infinite A->B->A loop. Consequence: the described fix only breaks single-integration echo, not the general issue-sync cycle.

true_positives.golden_comment: MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from StatefulDetectorHandler but only contains pass, failing to implement its required abstract methods: counter_names (property), get_dedupe_value(), get_group_key_values(), and build_occurrence_and_event_data(). This will cause a TypeError at runtime when the class is instantiated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now abstract and cannot be instantiated

MetricAlertDetectorHandler was changed to subclass StatefulDetectorHandler but provides no implementations. StatefulDetectorHandler declares abstract members counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and the new build_occurrence_and_event_data. A subclass that does not override them remains abstract, so group_type.detector_handler(self) in src/sentry/workflow_engine/models/detector.py will raise TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class. process_detectors does not catch this, so any detector of this type will crash evaluation instead of being skipped.

true_positives.golden_comment: Docstring says this returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult, but the method now returns a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey. Consider updating the docstring to match the new return type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
evaluate docstring still says list after change to dict

StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate was changed to return dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult], but its docstring still says it returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult with one result per group key. Readers of only the docstring will expect the old contract.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Wrong value `6` passed for `group_2` occurrence — the data packet specifies `"group_2": 10`. Should be `10` to accurately reflect the test scenario, which will ensure the test produces the correct occurrence data.

false_positives.candidate:
get_state_data KeyErrors when counter_names is empty

get_state_data initializes counter_updates as {} and only populates it inside if self.counter_names:. The result construction unconditionally does counter_updates[gk]. When a detector defines counter_names as an empty list, which the if-guard explicitly anticipates, this raises KeyError for every group key. The fallback for no counters should be None or {} per key, not a missing dict entry.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The function modifies the config variable to include display values but then returns the original monitor.config instead of the modified version.
The code fetches MonitorCheckIn objects by ID when the required data already exists in previous_checkins. This creates an unnecessary database query.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Inconsistent metric tag shard vs shards

SpanFlusher.main emits spans.buffer.flusher.produce with tags={"shard": shard_tag} on line 185 but spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce with tags={"shards": shard_tag} on line 199. Dashboards and alerts grouping by shard will miss half the timers. Use the same tag key in both timers.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() abandons remaining flusher processes on timeout

In SpanFlusher.join() the loop computes remaining_time and does break when the deadline expires. Breaking exits the for loop entirely, so any processes not yet waited on are never joined nor terminated and join() returns while workers are still alive. The single-process predecessor always waited then terminated its worker. The loop should continue to terminate remaining workers or record that shutdown timed out, not silently leave them running.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

false_positives.candidate:
Flusher restart leaks old worker and double-flushes shards

In _ensure_processes_alive the old worker is replaced via _create_process_for_shards() immediately after process.kill() without join()/close(). For the threading.Thread test path the isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) guard is false so nothing stops the old thread at all. The old worker keeps looping on the same shards while the new worker starts, so two workers call buffer.flush_segments()/done_flush_segments() and produce() for the same shards concurrently, causing duplicate Kafka produces and racing Redis deletes. Kill must be followed by join/close and threads must be stopped before replacement.

Multi-process flusher test never flushes

test_flusher_processes_limit creates 4 partitions with flusher_processes=2, asserts process counts and shard totals, then joins without submitting any spans, advancing drift, or checking output, backpressure, or per-process shard assignment. It cannot catch duplicate production, lost shards, or the restart/join bugs introduced by sharding. Extend it to write spans on multiple shards and verify each segment is produced exactly once.

Zero/negative flusher_processes silently disables flushing

In SpanFlusher.__init__ num_processes is min(max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards)) with max_processes = max_processes or len(...). A value of 0 falls back to len() silently, a negative value is truthy so num_processes becomes negative, range(negative) is empty and no processes are created. With empty assigned_shards num_processes is also 0. In all these cases submit() still accepts messages and advances drift but no background process ever calls flush_segments(), so segments sit in Redis forever with no error. Validate max_processes >=1 and assigned_shards non-empty or fall back to 1 process.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

false_positives.candidate:
Commit scan loops over offset gaps

In src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets iterates range(start, max_offset+1) to find contiguous completion. If offsets are sparse (e.g. 100 and 1_000_100 after a gap, filtering, or different assignment), it loops ~1M times per partition on every 1s commit tick. Consequence is CPU burn and stalled commit thread, delaying all commits.

Failed work is still marked complete and committed

In src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py OrderedQueueWorker.run catches all Exceptions from result_processor, logs, then unconditionally calls offset_tracker.complete_offset in finally. The class docstring claims only successful processing is committed. Consequence is a poison or transient failure advances the committed offset past the failed message, so the message is lost with no retry or DLQ.

Partition lock creation is racy

In src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py OffsetTracker._get_partition_lock does get then setdefault on partition_locks dict with no global lock. Two threads for the same new Partition can both miss the get and create different Lock objects, so add_offset/complete_offset/get_committable_offsets for that partition can run under different locks. Consequence is corrupted all_offsets/outstanding sets and wrong committable offsets, causing duplicate processing or skipping offsets.

Shared queue pool is shut down by per-partition strategy

In src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/result_consumer.py create_thread_queue_parallel_worker shares factory.queue_pool across all strategies from create_with_partitions, but SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close/terminate calls queue_pool.shutdown. Closing one partition assignment (e.g. on rebalance) kills workers for all current and future assignments reusing the factory pool, after which submit either blocks or raises queue.ShutDown and messages stop being processed.

Shutdown abandons queued work

In src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown=True before draining, and OrderedQueueWorker.run exits when that flag is set after the current item. Remaining queued WorkItems are never processed and their offsets never completed. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close calls this path, so normal close/rebalance drops in-memory work and forces redelivery or stalls commits.

Unbounded queues provide no backpressure

In src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() with no maxsize while claiming natural backpressure. If a queue's worker stalls on a slow subscription, submit keeps appending via non-blocking put. Consequence is unbounded memory growth and OOM, instead of blocking the Arroyo poll loop.

join ignores timeout and always closes

In src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(timeout) ignores the timeout argument and unconditionally calls close, which joins the commit thread for 5s and shuts down the pool. Callers expecting Arroyo join semantics (wait up to timeout without destroying the strategy) instead get a destructive shutdown.

wait_until_empty ignores in-flight work

In src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty and get_stats use only Queue.qsize. An item taken by a worker but not yet finished or offset-completed leaves qsize at 0. Consequence is callers conclude processing is done while work is still in flight, causing premature commits checks and flaky tests.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Every cached deny now forces a full DB permission fetch

Check first reads getCachedIdentityPermissions and, if the cached scope map does not contain the resource, unconditionally calls getIdentityPermissions. The cache-hit fast paths were removed from getUserPermissions and getAnonymousPermissions, so that call always queries basic roles, teams and permissions from the DB. Previously a fresh permCache hit decided allow/deny without I/O. Now any user without access to a resource hits the DB on first Check per resource, and scanning N distinct denied resources causes N DB permission builds (only the second identical-resource hit is absorbed by the denial cache). This turns deny-heavy workloads into a DB storm.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-precedence test stores false instead of true

TestService_CacheCheck 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' seeds permCache with map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false} and claims this proves the denial entry is checked instead of the allow. Since checkPermission treats a false map value the same as missing (it tests truthiness), both caches deny. The test never exercises denial-wins-over-allow. It should seed map value true, otherwise a regression that ignores permDenialCache would still pass.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial-cache key omits identity type, causing cross-identity false denies

In Service.Check the denial key is built as userPermDenialCacheKey(namespace, userUID, action, name, parent) with no identity type. Anonymous subject 'anonymous:0' and renderer subject 'render:0' both resolve to UID '0', and user vs service-account UIDs can also collide as strings. A denial cached for one identity type (e.g. anonymous denied dashboards:read on dash1) will therefore hit for a different identity type on the same namespace/action/resource (e.g. renderer, which is allowed dashboards:read/folders:read) and Check returns Allowed:false without consulting permissions. The fix is to include IdentityType in the denial key.

List still serves stale cached permissions with no DB fallback

Check was changed to fall back to the DB when cached permissions do not contain the requested resource, but List was changed to use getCachedIdentityPermissions with no equivalent fallback: on a permCache hit it directly calls listPermission. A newly granted dashboard/folder will therefore be missing from List results for up to shortCacheTTL while Check already allows it, leaving Check and List inconsistent and the creator flow still broken for listings.

Negative caching reintroduces stale denies for newly granted access

Service.Check caches every deny in permDenialCache for shortCacheTTL (30s) and short-circuits future Checks on a hit before reading permissions. If a user is denied and then granted access to the same dashboard/folder (the exact creator flow this PR fixes, role/team/assignment change, or folder-tree refresh), subsequent Checks within the TTL incorrectly return denied without hitting the DB. The fast deny path defeats the new fallback-to-DB logic for the most important transition from deny to allow.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing React key on Grafana list item

In FilterViewResults the grafana branch renders <GrafanaRuleListItem> without key={key} while the datasource and unknown branches do pass key. Without a stable key React cannot reconcile the infinite-scroll list correctly, causing duplicate-key warnings, wrong item reuse/state preservation and extra re-mounts when pages load.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence drawer never opens for prom-only rules

RuleActionsButtons allows Silence via useGrafanaPromRuleAbility on promRule alone, calling setShowSilenceDrawer(true), but the drawer is rendered only if rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) where rule is the optional RulerRuleDTO. In the new Grafana list view rule is undefined, so the condition is always false and clicking Silence does nothing. The menu offers an action that has no effect.

false_positives.candidate:
Creating/deleting states silently dropped

GrafanaGroupLoader no longer fetches the ruler group or runs matchRules. Rules that exist only in ruler (just created, Prometheus not yet synced) now disappear entirely instead of showing Creating, and rules deleted from ruler but still in Prometheus now render as normal instead of Deleting. Users see stale normal rows that will fail on edit/delete, or missing rows with no explanation.

Federated rule protection removed

useAllRulerRuleAbilities previously set immutableRule using isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) to block Edit/Delete/Pause on federated Mimir groups. The PR replaces it with const isFederated = false with a TODO. Federated groups are now treated as mutable, so users will be offered Edit/Delete/Pause on rules that must be immutable, risking failed API calls or unintended mutations.

Pause action can never show in ruler-less list view

AlertRuleMenu computes canPause as ruler-ability OR grafana-prom-ability to support the list view without ruler data, but the Pause menu item is still gated on rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule). When rulerRule is undefined (the new list view) that predicate is false, so Pause is never rendered even when canPause is true via promRule. Users with pause permission lose the Pause/Unpause action.

Prom-only non-Grafana rules lose all actions

getEditableIdentifier returns undefined for a prom-only rule that is not a Grafana prom rule, and RuleActionsButtons returns null in that case. That removes the entire Stack including the More menu (Copy link, Silence, etc.), not just Edit. Any consumer rendering a cloud Prometheus-only rule without ruler data gets no actions at all.

Provisioned check fails open when provenance missing

isProvisionedPromRule returns Boolean(promRule.provenance) and the new provenance field on GrafanaPromRuleDTOBase is optional. Any response without that field (older server, cache, mock) evaluates to false, so provisioned Grafana rules are classified as editable/removable/pausable. Combined with the new prom-only abilities path, provisioned rules can show Edit/Duplicate/Delete/Pause in the list view.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
Empty check runs on raw expr instead of interpolated expr

In querySplitting.ts runSplitQuery filters !hide and query.expr before calling datasource.applyTemplateVariables. A query like expr '$expr' is non-empty before interpolation but can become '' after interpolation. Because the empty filter already ran, the query is kept, grouped, split and sent to runQuery instead of being ignored like other empty queries. This wastes requests and can send invalid empty selectors to the backend.

Filter-before-interpolate lets empty-after-interpolation queries through

In shardQuerySplitting.ts runShardSplitQuery changed from interpolateVariablesInQueries(...).filter(expr).filter(!hide) to request.targets.filter(expr).filter(!hide).map(applyTemplateVariables). If a variable expands to empty (e.g. expr '$var' with empty value) the old code dropped the query after interpolation, the new code keeps it because emptiness is tested on the raw expr. That causes needless fetchLabelValues for __stream_shard__ with a bad selector and downstream shard sub-queries with empty selectors.

Interpolating before range-variable guard defeats no-split rule

In querySplitting.ts runSplitQuery now does .filter(expr).map(applyTemplateVariables) and then partitions with querySupportsSplitting which checks !isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr). Because applyTemplateVariables expands template variables via replace (as the new test shows for $__auto/$step), an expr containing $__range/$__range_s/$__range_ms no longer contains that marker after interpolation. The guard therefore never fires and range-variable queries that must not be split are split. All split sub-requests then reuse the full-range interpolated value instead of each split range getting its own $__range, returning incorrect data.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing nil-request guard causes panic before LoggerMiddleware

ContextualLoggerMiddleware QueryData/CallResource/CheckHealth/CollectMetrics in contextual_logger_middleware.go dereference req.PluginContext and req fields unconditionally. LoggerMiddleware in the same package explicitly checks if req == nil and bypasses logging, proving nil requests are expected. Because ContextualLoggerMiddleware is ordered outer to LoggerMiddleware, a nil request panics in instrumentContext path before reaching the nil-safe logger.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext discards logged output

TestLogger.FromContext in pkg/plugins/log/fake.go returns NewTestLogger() instead of the receiver. LoggerMiddleware now does m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), so when tests inject a TestLogger the Info/Warn/Error call goes to a fresh throwaway instance. The original TestLogger under test never records Calls/Message/Ctx, making log assertions impossible and hiding regressions.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.

false_positives.candidate:
Adding FromContext to Logger interface breaks implementers

Logger interface in pkg/plugins/log/ifaces.go gains a new required method FromContext(ctx context.Context) Logger. Any existing implementation of plugins/log.Logger outside this PR (other mocks, wrappers, external code) will fail to compile. Adding a method to a public interface is a breaking API change and requires updating all implementers or providing a default.

When the API request completes the parent context is cancelled, which immediately cancels the child, so the best-effort legacy write can be aborted before it runs. The consequence is the legacy backup silently diverges. The async work must derive from a detached context (e.g. context.WithoutCancel or context.Background) plus timeout.

Two goroutines that both observe ret==nil can then both proceed to do file/CDN I/O sequentially and publish. This causes thundering-herd I/O on cold start and allows a later writer to overwrite a good value just published by an earlier writer, including overwriting it with a failure.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. Line 69 does entryPointAssetsCache = result even when readWebAssetsFromFile/CDN returned an error and result is nil. Combined with the missing re-check, a transient failure in one concurrent caller wipes a good EntryPointAssets value just cached by another caller, turning subsequent requests into errors and forcing repeated disk reads. Both NewSQLCommand and UnmarshalSQLCommand should fail fast with an explicit 'sql expressions disabled for security' error instead of attempting TablesList/QueryFramesInto.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Narrowed BuildIndex lock allows duplicate builds for same key

BuildIndex previously held cacheMu for the whole build, which serialized builds. It now only locks around b.cache[key] = idx. Two concurrent getOrCreateIndex calls for the same NamespacedResource can both observe a miss, both call bleve.New on the same file directory and both run the builder, then last-writer-wins in the map. The loser index is leaked, IndexTenants metrics are double-incremented, and concurrent bleve.New on the same path can fail or corrupt the on-disk index. A per-key singleflight or double-checked lock is needed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs reads cache map without lock

TotalDocs iterates b.cache with no RLock while BuildIndex concurrently does b.cache[key] = idx under Lock. Concurrent map read and write is a fatal data race in Go and can crash the process. It must hold cacheMu.RLock during iteration. The race window was widened by allowing concurrent builds.

false_positives.candidate:
Data race on shared err and counter in init workers

searchSupport.init launches one errgroup goroutine per namespace. Inside the closure it does totalBatchesIndexed++ and _, _, err = s.build(...) where err is the outer variable from GetResourceStats. Multiple goroutines read/write the same err variable and increment the same int with no synchronization. This is a data race that corrupts the error return and the indexed count and will be flagged by -race. Use a local variable and return it, and use an atomic counter.

History/Origin panic when search is not configured

Search checks if s.search == nil and returns an error, but History and Origin unconditionally call s.search.History and s.search.Origin. When Search.Resources is nil, newSearchSupport is skipped and s.search stays nil, so any History or Origin RPC causes a nil-pointer panic. Add the same nil guard as Search.

Removing per-RPC Init checks removes stop gate

All handlers previously called s.Init(ctx) which returned s.initErr, so after Stop set initErr to stopping/stopped, new Read/List/Create/Update/Delete/Watch/Search calls failed fast. After this change NewResourceServer calls Init once and handlers never consult initErr, so after Stop cancels the broadcaster context the server keeps serving reads and writes against the backend. Either re-check a stopped/failed flag per RPC or document that Stop no longer gates traffic.

Silently skipping postgres storage-server test

The test now skips when GRAFANA_TEST_DB is postgres with only a TODO comment. If eager Init at startup breaks postgres, this skip hides the regression and reduces coverage for exactly the backend this PR touches. The skip should be justified with a linked issue or removed before merge.

Watch loop uses Background context and ignores closed channel

searchSupport.init creates watchctx := context.Background() and then loops with v := <-events followed by handleEvent(watchctx, v). If the storage WatchWriteEvents channel closes, the receive returns nil forever, causing a hot infinite loop and a nil-pointer dereference inside handleEvent when it accesses evt.Type. The Background context is also never cancelled, so polling queries are not tied to server shutdown. Derive the watch context from the server context and check the ok result of the receive.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.
