true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider returns unrelated KeyStore provider

AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider() in AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, typically the JDK SUN provider, and presents it as the BouncyCastle provider. Callers that expect a BC/BCFIPS provider name or BC-specific algorithms via BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER will get the wrong provider, causing NoSuchAlgorithmException or silently using a different implementation. true_positives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
readSequence accepts indefinite length and trailing garbage

ASN1Decoder.readSequence() in ASN1Decoder.java calls readLength() which can return -1 for indefinite-length encoding 0x80, but readSequence() does not reject -1 and will return an empty list, later reported only as size != 2. It also never verifies that the declared sequence length was exactly consumed and that no trailing bytes remain after the sequence. Consequence is malformed DER signatures with indefinite lengths or appended garbage can be accepted into the ECDSA conversion path instead of being strictly rejected as required for DER.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New order() method has no default and breaks external implementations

CryptoProvider.java adds `int order()` without a default implementation. Every existing out-of-tree implementation of CryptoProvider will now fail to compile/link with NoSuchMethodError. The in-tree DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider were updated, but third-party providers were not. Consequence is a breaking API change; it should be a `default` method (e.g. default 0/100) to remain backwards compatible.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.

false_positives.candidate:
ECDSA conversion does not validate lengths and silently truncates

In AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java, concatenatedRSToASN1DER() assumes signature.length == signLength without checking and will throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException on malformed input instead of IOException. Conversely asn1derToConcatenatedRS()/integerToBytes() truncates when BigInteger is negative or larger than qLength by copying only the low bytes without any check. Consequence is malformed or attacker-controlled DER signatures are silently mapped to a different valid-looking raw R||S value instead of being rejected, which is a signature-parsing integrity risk. Both directions must validate sizes and sign and throw IOException.

Multiple crypto providers silently ignored instead of failing

detectProvider() in CryptoIntegration.java previously threw IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath. It now sorts by order() and silently picks the first, logging only at debug level. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200, so if e.g. both default and FIPS jars are present the choice among equals is ServiceLoader-order dependent and non-deterministic. Consequence is misconfiguration (notably FIPS vs non-FIPS) is now hidden and the server may run with the wrong crypto stack without any warning.

Test reuses P-256 key for ES384/ES512 and never verifies signature

ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java generates one EC KeyPair with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` (default P-256/secp256r1) in the constructor and reuses it for ES256, ES384 and ES512 tests. The ES384/ES512 cases therefore do not exercise real P-384/P-521 keys and lengths (e.g. 96/132 byte R||S), only zero-padded P-256 values. The test also only checks round-trip rs->DER->rs equality and never verifies the converted DER with Signature.verify() or compares to JCA output. Consequence is the test passes while giving false confidence about interop for larger curves and about correctness of the DER encoding.

The Background context is also never cancelled, so polling queries are not tied to server shutdown. Derive the watch context from the server context and check the ok result of the receive.

History/Origin panic when search is not configured

Search checks if s.search == nil and returns an error, but History and Origin unconditionally call s.search.History and s.search.Origin. When Search.Resources is nil, newSearchSupport is skipped and s.search stays nil, so any History or Origin RPC causes a nil-pointer panic. Add the same nil guard as Search.

Removing per-RPC Init checks removes stop gate

All handlers previously called s.Init(ctx) which returned s.initErr, so after Stop set initErr to stopping/stopped, new Read/List/Create/Update/Delete/Watch/Search calls failed fast. After this change NewResourceServer calls Init once and handlers never consult initErr, so after Stop cancels the broadcaster context the server keeps serving reads and writes against the backend. Either re-check a stopped/failed flag per RPC or document that Stop no longer gates traffic.

Silently skipping postgres storage-server test

The test now skips when GRAFANA_TEST_DB is postgres with only a TODO comment. If eager Init at startup breaks postgres, this skip hides the regression and reduces coverage for exactly the backend this PR touches. The skip should be justified with a linked issue or removed before merge.

In checkIfIsAvailable the code tests `dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...)` to detect a zero-length date override (day marked unavailable). `dayjs()` returns an object, so `===` compares object identity and is always false. As a result a full-day block is never detected, `dateOverrideExist` stays true and the function later returns true (available). true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: using the strict equality operator (`===`) to compare two `dayjs` objects (`dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...)`), which compares object references rather than their underlying date values and therefore always evaluates to false.

false_positives.candidate:
Working-hours check fails with split hours

In checkIfIsAvailable availability is rejected if `workingHours.find(workingHour => slot is outside that workingHour)` finds any entry. If a user has two intervals on the same weekday (e.g. morning and afternoon), a slot inside one interval is outside the other, so `find` always succeeds and every slot is marked unavailable. The correct test is that a slot is available if it is inside any interval, not that it is outside any interval. Fixed hosts with split hours will show no slots.

Date-override containment misses slots overflowing the override

In checkIfIsAvailable a slot is deemed outside a date override only if `slotEnd <= overrideStart` or `slotStart > overrideEnd`. A slot that starts inside the override but ends after `override.end` (e.g. override 10:00-11:00, slot 10:30-11:30) satisfies neither condition, so `find` returns undefined and the slot is treated as inside the override and returned as available. This allows bookings that extend beyond the override window. The same block also uses `isAfter` instead of same-or-after for the end boundary, so a slot starting exactly at override end is treated as inside.

Timezone offset computed from Date.toString()

In getSlots the offsets are computed as `dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone)` and `.tz(timeZone)`. `Date.toString()` produces a locale-dependent string without explicit offset that dayjs must re-parse, which can lose the original instant, depend on server locale, and give the wrong `utcOffset()` around DST. The Date object should be passed directly to dayjs, e.g. `dayjs(override.start).tz(...)`, to preserve the instant.

Date-override timezone shift drops day rollover

In getSlots an override is converted to invitee minutes-since-midnight via `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset).hour()*60+minute`. Only hour/minute are kept and the result is applied to the original `startOfInviteeDay`. If the invitee-organizer offset moves the override across midnight, the portion belonging to the adjacent invitee day is still placed on the original day (or `start >= end` and skipped entirely). This creates slots on the wrong day or drops availability for timezones far apart.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() abandons remaining flusher processes on timeout

In SpanFlusher.join() the loop computes remaining_time and does break when the deadline expires. Breaking exits the for loop entirely, so any processes not yet waited on are never joined nor terminated and join() returns while workers are still alive. The single-process predecessor always waited then terminated its worker. The loop should continue to terminate remaining workers or record that shutdown timed out, not silently leave them running.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that breaking out of the join loop when the deadline expires skips termination of remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown.

false_positives.candidate:
Zero/negative flusher_processes silently disables flushing

In SpanFlusher.__init__ num_processes is min(max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards)) with max_processes = max_processes or len(...). A value of 0 falls back to len() silently, a negative value is truthy so num_processes becomes negative, range(negative) is empty and no processes are created. With empty assigned_shards num_processes is also 0. In all these cases submit() still accepts messages and advances drift but no background process ever calls flush_segments(), so segments sit in Redis forever with no error. Validate max_processes >=1 and assigned_shards non-empty or fall back to 1 process.

Flusher restart leaks old worker and double-flushes shards

In _ensure_processes_alive the old worker is replaced via _create_process_for_shards() immediately after process.kill() without join()/close(). For the threading.Thread test path the isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) guard is false so nothing stops the old thread at all. The old worker keeps looping on the same shards while the new worker starts, so two workers call buffer.flush_segments()/done_flush_segments() and produce() for the same shards concurrently, causing duplicate Kafka produces and racing Redis deletes. Kill must be followed by join/close and threads must be stopped before replacement.

Multi-process flusher test never flushes

test_flusher_processes_limit creates 4 partitions with flusher_processes=2, asserts process counts and shard totals, then joins without submitting any spans, advancing drift, or checking output, backpressure, or per-process shard assignment. It cannot catch duplicate production, lost shards, or the restart/join bugs introduced by sharding. Extend it to write spans on multiple shards and verify each segment is produced exactly once.

TestService_CacheCheck 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' seeds permCache with map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false} and claims this proves the denial entry is checked instead of the allow. Since checkPermission treats a false map value the same as missing (it tests truthiness), both caches deny. The test never exercises denial-wins-over-allow. It should seed map value true, otherwise a regression that ignores permDenialCache would still pass.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that the test claims the permission cache allows access but seeds dashboards:uid:dash1 with false, which checkPermission treats as not allowed. The candidate explains the resulting failure to test denial precedence, matching the same underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial-cache key omits identity type, causing cross-identity false denies

In Service.Check the denial key is built as userPermDenialCacheKey(namespace, userUID, action, name, parent) with no identity type. Anonymous subject 'anonymous:0' and renderer subject 'render:0' both resolve to UID '0', and user vs service-account UIDs can also collide as strings. A denial cached for one identity type (e.g. anonymous denied dashboards:read on dash1) will therefore hit for a different identity type on the same namespace/action/resource (e.g. renderer, which is allowed dashboards:read/folders:read) and Check returns Allowed:false without consulting permissions. The fix is to include IdentityType in the denial key.

Negative caching reintroduces stale denies for newly granted access

Service.Check caches every deny in permDenialCache for shortCacheTTL (30s) and short-circuits future Checks on a hit before reading permissions. If a user is denied and then granted access to the same dashboard/folder (the exact creator flow this PR fixes, role/team/assignment change, or folder-tree refresh), subsequent Checks within the TTL incorrectly return denied without hitting the DB. The fast deny path defeats the new fallback-to-DB logic for the most important transition from deny to allow.

Every cached deny now forces a full DB permission fetch

Check first reads getCachedIdentityPermissions and, if the cached scope map does not contain the resource, unconditionally calls getIdentityPermissions. The cache-hit fast paths were removed from getUserPermissions and getAnonymousPermissions, so that call always queries basic roles, teams and permissions from the DB. Previously a fresh permCache hit decided allow/deny without I/O. Now any user without access to a resource hits the DB on first Check per resource, and scanning N distinct denied resources causes N DB permission builds (only the second identical-resource hit is absorbed by the denial cache). This turns deny-heavy workloads into a DB storm.

List still serves stale cached permissions with no DB fallback

Check was changed to fall back to the DB when cached permissions do not contain the requested resource, but List was changed to use getCachedIdentityPermissions with no equivalent fallback: on a permCache hit it directly calls listPermission. A newly granted dashboard/folder will therefore be missing from List results for up to shortCacheTTL while Check already allows it, leaving Check and List inconsistent and the creator flow still broken for listings.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:

In checkIfIsAvailable the code tests `dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...)` to detect a zero-length date override (day marked unavailable). `dayjs()` returns an object, so `===` compares object identity and is always false. As a result a full-day block is never detected, `dateOverrideExist` stays true and the function later returns true (available). A day the host blocked off will still show bookable slots and can be booked.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: using === to compare separately created Dayjs objects compares references rather than date values, so the equality check always fails. The candidate adds consequences but describes the same underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Working-hours check fails with split hours

In checkIfIsAvailable availability is rejected if `workingHours.find(workingHour => slot is outside that workingHour)` finds any entry. If a user has two intervals on the same weekday (e.g. morning and afternoon), a slot inside one interval is outside the other, so `find` always succeeds and every slot is marked unavailable. The correct test is that a slot is available if it is inside any interval, not that it is outside any interval. Fixed hosts with split hours will show no slots.

Date-override containment misses slots overflowing the override

In checkIfIsAvailable a slot is deemed outside a date override only if `slotEnd <= overrideStart` or `slotStart > overrideEnd`. A slot that starts inside the override but ends after `override.end` (e.g. override 10:00-11:00, slot 10:30-11:30) satisfies neither condition, so `find` returns undefined and the slot is treated as inside the override and returned as available. This allows bookings that extend beyond the override window. The same block also uses `isAfter` instead of same-or-after for the end boundary, so a slot starting exactly at override end is treated as inside.

Timezone offset computed from Date.toString()

In getSlots the offsets are computed as `dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone)` and `.tz(timeZone)`. `Date.toString()` produces a locale-dependent string without explicit offset that dayjs must re-parse, which can lose the original instant, depend on server locale, and give the wrong `utcOffset()` around DST. The Date object should be passed directly to dayjs, e.g. `dayjs(override.start).tz(...)`, to preserve the instant.

Date-override timezone shift drops day rollover

In getSlots an override is converted to invitee minutes-since-midnight via `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset).hour()*60+minute`. Only hour/minute are kept and the result is applied to the original `startOfInviteeDay`. If the invitee-organizer offset moves the override across midnight, the portion belonging to the adjacent invitee day is still placed on the original day (or `start >= end` and skipped entirely). This creates slots on the wrong day or drops availability for timezones far apart.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() abandons remaining flusher processes on timeout

In SpanFlusher.join() the loop computes remaining_time and does break when the deadline expires. Breaking exits the for loop entirely, so any processes not yet waited on are never joined nor terminated and join() returns while workers are still alive. The single-process predecessor always waited then terminated its worker. The loop should continue to terminate remaining workers or record that shutdown timed out, not silently leave them running.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same problem: breaking out of the join loop once the deadline passes means the remaining flusher processes are never terminated and keep running after shutdown.

false_positives.candidate:
Zero/negative flusher_processes silently disables flushing

In SpanFlusher.__init__ num_processes is min(max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards)) with max_processes = max_processes or len(...). A value of 0 falls back to len() silently, a negative value is truthy so num_processes becomes negative, range(negative) is empty and no processes are created. With empty assigned_shards num_processes is also 0. In all these cases submit() still accepts messages and advances drift but no background process ever calls flush_segments(), so segments sit in Redis forever with no error. Validate max_processes >=1 and assigned_shards non-empty or fall back to 1 process.

Flusher restart leaks old worker and double-flushes shards

In _ensure_processes_alive the old worker is replaced via _create_process_for_shards() immediately after process.kill() without join()/close(). For the threading.Thread test path the isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) guard is false so nothing stops the old thread at all. The old worker keeps looping on the same shards while the new worker starts, so two workers call buffer.flush_segments()/done_flush_segments() and produce() for the same shards concurrently, causing duplicate Kafka produces and racing Redis deletes. Kill must be followed by join/close and threads must be stopped before replacement.

Multi-process flusher test never flushes

test_flusher_processes_limit creates 4 partitions with flusher_processes=2, asserts process counts and shard totals, then joins without submitting any spans, advancing drift, or checking output, backpressure, or per-process shard assignment. It cannot catch duplicate production, lost shards, or the restart/join bugs introduced by sharding. Extend it to write spans on multiple shards and verify each segment is produced exactly once.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

The test starts a background thread that loops while(!deletedAll.get()) calling the admin API, then deletes groups, sets deletedAll to true, and immediately asserts caughtExceptions is empty without joining the thread. The assert can run while the reader is still in-flight, so a failure occurring after the assert is missed (false pass) and the thread can leak into the next test. If the delete loop throws, deletedAll is never set and the thread spins forever. The tight loop with no pause/backoff also floods the server with Integer.MAX_VALUE queries.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same problem: the reader thread is never joined, so asserting right after setting deletedAll is racy and can miss exceptions. The candidate's extra points don't change that core match.

false_positives.candidate:
Sibling getSubGroupsStream methods still NPE on concurrent delete

The PR fixes NPE in getSubGroupsCount() by null-checking modelSupplier.get(), but the three overloads getSubGroupsStream(search,first,max), getSubGroupsStream(first,max) and getSubGroupsStream(search,exact,first,max) still do modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...) with no null check. If the group is deleted concurrently before the lazy supplier is first loaded, get() returns null and these methods throw NullPointerException, causing the same 500 failure the PR claims to fix. They need the same null handling as getSubGroupsCount().

false_negatives.golden_comment: Returning null from getSubGroupsCount() violates the GroupModel contract (Javadoc says it never returns null) and may lead to NPEs in callers that expect a non-null count.

true_positives.golden_comment: In UsernameForm.authenticate(), isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() is called without passing the required UserModel parameter.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Call to non-existent zero-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled breaks compilation

UsernameForm.java line 47 calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments. The only definition in the superclass UsernamePasswordForm is isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) requiring one argument. There is no zero-arg overload. The code cannot compile, breaking the whole services module. It should pass the user, e.g. isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser()).
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug: UsernameForm calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments, but the method requires a UserModel parameter.

true_positives.golden_comment: With isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) requiring user != null, authenticate(...) will not call webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) on the initial login page where context.getUser() is still null, so conditional passkey UI will not be set up for first-time passkey login. Consider whether this should also be enabled when no user has been selected yet so ID-less passkey authentication on the initial login form continues to work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Passkeys conditional UI now requires a known user, disabling it on initial login

isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) returns webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled() && user != null. It is used in authenticate() and challenge() to decide whether to call webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context). Previously the code filled the form when passkeys were enabled and context.getUser() == null (initial login). Now it only fills when context.getUser() != null (re-authentication). Initial login with no user therefore never gets ENABLE_WEBAUTHN_CONDITIONAL_UI, challenge, RP ID or webauth form, breaking username-less / conditional-UI passkey login. The PR's own tests still expect //form[@id='webauth'] on the first page.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same problem. The user != null check in isConditionalPasskeysEnabled stops fillContextForm from being called on the initial login page, where no user is set yet. That breaks conditional passkey login without a username.

false_positives.candidate:
Re-authentication attributes set on throwaway form instance are lost

setupReauthenticationInUsernamePasswordFormError() does LoginFormsProvider form = context.form(); form.setAttribute(USERNAME_HIDDEN,true); form.setAttribute(REGISTRATION_DISABLED,true); and then returns. The caller in AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator.badPasswordHandler() and WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator.createErrorResponse() then creates a different instance via challenge()/errorChallenge.apply() which internally calls context.form() again. Each context.form() returns a new LoginFormsProvider, so attributes set on the first instance never reach the rendered response. After a failed password/passkey during re-authentication the page will show the regular login with editable username and registration link instead of hidden-username re-authentication.

Error response discards webauthn form state via multiple context.form() instances

createErrorResponse() calls context.form().setError(...), context.form().setAttribute(...), AuthenticatorUtils.setup...(context) which uses another context.form(), fillContextForm(context) whose returned LoginFormsProvider with new challenge and attributes is discarded, then return errorChallenge.apply(context) which builds yet another fresh form. Because each context.form() is a new instance, the error, ENABLE_WEBAUTHN_CONDITIONAL_UI flag, and the fresh challenge/attributes never make it into the returned Response. On passkey failure the user gets a page without the error displayed and without valid conditional-UI data, and the auth-session challenge note does not match what was rendered.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative queryset slice crashes instead of paginating

In src/sentry/api/paginator.py OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result allows start_offset=cursor.offset when enable_advanced_features and offset<0, then does queryset[start_offset:stop]. Django QuerySets explicitly reject negative indexing with AssertionError/ValueError, they do not wrap like Python lists. The comment claiming Django handles negative slicing automatically is false. Consequence: an attacker-controlled cursor string like value:-10:0 reaches an unhandled exception and returns 500, a remotely triggerable availability issue.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator uses negative slice offsets on Django querysets, which Django rejects with an error. The golden comment names organization_auditlogs.py, where the paginator is used. The candidate names paginator.py, where it is defined. The underlying issue is identical.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator breaks datetime ordering

In src/sentry/api/paginator.py OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does math.floor/ceil directly on getattr(item, self.key) and value_from_cursor returns cursor.value as int. The only caller in src/sentry/api/endpoints/organization_auditlogs.py uses order_by="-datetime", so the key is a datetime object. math.floor(datetime) raises TypeError and filtering a datetime column against int 0 in build_queryset is a type mismatch. Consequence: any request with optimized_pagination=true crashes with 500 or paginates incorrectly instead of behaving like DateTimePaginator.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate points to the same bug as the golden comment: get_item_key calls math.floor/ceil on a datetime key because the audit logs endpoint uses order_by=-datetime, which raises a TypeError.

false_positives.candidate:
Unknown paginate kwarg enable_advanced_features

In src/sentry/api/endpoints/organization_auditlogs.py the optimized branch calls self.paginate(..., paginator_cls=OptimizedCursorPaginator, enable_advanced_features=True). Base endpoint paginate does not define that parameter and does not forward arbitrary kwargs to the paginator constructor in the established codebase. Consequence: the optimized path either raises TypeError for unexpected keyword argument returning 500, or silently drops the flag so the paginator never actually enables the intended mode, making the branch dead/broken.

Global BasePaginator offset clamp is inconsistent and wrong

In src/sentry/api/paginator.py BasePaginator.get_result was changed for all APIs from queryset[offset:offset+limit+extra] to start_offset=max(0,offset) for forward cursors but keeps raw offset for is_prev cursors and for the later check len(results)==offset+limit+extra. Other paginators in the same file (OffsetPaginator, ChainPaginator, CombinedQuerysetPaginator) reject offset<0 with BadPaginationError (400). Consequence: this global change silently coerces invalid forward cursors to page 0 instead of 400, still crashes for is_prev negative offsets, and miscomputes has_more when clamping because the length check uses the unclamped offset.

New paginator and endpoint branch have no tests

In src/sentry/api/paginator.py a new OptimizedCursorPaginator class and a modified BasePaginator path plus a new optimized_pagination branch in OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint were added with no unit or API tests. Consequence: the datetime-key crash, negative-slice crash, and paginate-kwarg mismatch above are uncaught, and future changes to global pagination have no regression coverage.

false_negatives.golden_comment: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Narrowed BuildIndex lock allows duplicate builds for same key

BuildIndex previously held cacheMu for the whole build, which serialized builds. It now only locks around b.cache[key] = idx. Two concurrent getOrCreateIndex calls for the same NamespacedResource can both observe a miss, both call bleve.New on the same file directory and both run the builder, then last-writer-wins in the map. The loser index is leaked, IndexTenants metrics are double-incremented, and concurrent bleve.New on the same path can fail or corrupt the on-disk index. A per-key singleflight or double-checked lock is needed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same issue: the cacheMu lock in BuildIndex was narrowed from covering the whole function to only the cache assignment, which lets concurrent duplicate builds of the same key happen. The candidate also adds further consequences of that race.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs reads cache map without lock

TotalDocs iterates b.cache with no RLock while BuildIndex concurrently does b.cache[key] = idx under Lock. Concurrent map read and write is a fatal data race in Go and can crash the process. It must hold cacheMu.RLock during iteration. The race window was widened by allowing concurrent builds.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. TotalDocs iterates b.cache without a lock while BuildIndex writes to the map concurrently, which can cause a concurrent map read/write panic. The golden comment adds the call-site context of the event watcher goroutine, but the core issue is identical.

false_positives.candidate:
Data race on shared err and counter in init workers

searchSupport.init launches one errgroup goroutine per namespace. Inside the closure it does totalBatchesIndexed++ and _, _, err = s.build(...) where err is the outer variable from GetResourceStats. Multiple goroutines read/write the same err variable and increment the same int with no synchronization. This is a data race that corrupts the error return and the indexed count and will be flagged by -race. Use a local variable and return it, and use an atomic counter.

Watch loop uses Background context and ignores closed channel

searchSupport.init creates watchctx := context.Background() and then loops with v := <-events followed by handleEvent(watchctx, v). If the storage WatchWriteEvents channel closes, the receive returns nil forever, causing a hot infinite loop and a nil-pointer dereference inside handleEvent when it accesses evt.Type. The Background context is also never cancelled, so polling queries are not tied to server shutdown. Derive the watch context from the server context and check the ok result of the receive.

History/Origin panic when search is not configured

Search checks if s.search == nil and returns an error, but History and Origin unconditionally call s.search.History and s.search.Origin. When Search.Resources is nil, newSearchSupport is skipped and s.search stays nil, so any History or Origin RPC causes a nil-pointer panic. Add the same nil guard as Search.

Removing per-RPC Init checks removes stop gate

All handlers previously called s.Init(ctx) which returned s.initErr, so after Stop set initErr to stopping/stopped, new Read/List/Create/Update/Delete/Watch/Search calls failed fast. After this change NewResourceServer calls Init once and handlers never consult initErr, so after Stop cancels the broadcaster context the server keeps serving reads and writes against the backend. Either re-check a stopped/failed flag per RPC or document that Stop no longer gates traffic.

Silently skipping postgres storage-server test

The test now skips when GRAFANA_TEST_DB is postgres with only a TODO comment. If eager Init at startup breaks postgres, this skip hides the regression and reduces coverage for exactly the backend this PR touches. The skip should be justified with a linked issue or removed before merge.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
queued default evaluated once at import time

In src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py the field is declared as `queued: datetime = timezone.now()`. The call to timezone.now() runs once when the module is imported, so every AssignmentSource created without an explicit queued value shares the same timestamp. It should be `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`. Consequence: provenance timestamps are wrong and any future debounce / ordering logic based on queued will be broken.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same bug: the `queued` default calls timezone.now() once when the class is defined or the module is imported, so every instance shares one timestamp. The candidate also gives the fix, default_factory.

true_positives.golden_comment: to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
to_dict/from_dict datetime does not survive task queue round-trip

AssignmentSource.to_dict() in src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py uses dataclasses.asdict, which leaves `queued` as a datetime object. src/sentry/integrations/utils/sync.py puts that dict into `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async` kwargs, which must be JSON serializable for Celery. After JSON round-trip the value comes back as a string, and AssignmentSource.from_dict() does `cls(**input_dict)` with no parsing, so `queued` becomes a str violating the declared datetime type. Consequence: task enqueue can fail or produce type-confused objects; serialization should use isoformat and parse back.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same problem. to_dict() returns a datetime for queued, the dict is passed into apply_async kwargs, and JSON serialization can then fail at enqueue. The candidate adds detail about the from_dict round-trip, but its core issue is identical.

false_positives.candidate:
Same-integration check does not stop multi-integration ping-pong

In src/sentry/integrations/mixins/issues.py should_sync() returns False only when `sync_source.integration_id == self.org_integration.integration_id`. src/sentry/integrations/utils/sync.py fans outbound assignee sync out to every GroupLink for the group. If one Sentry group is linked to two different integrations A and B, an inbound assign from A is blocked from echoing to A but still syncs to B, B's webhook then re-enters as inbound from B and syncs to A, forming an infinite A->B->A loop. Consequence: the described fix only breaks single-integration echo, not the general issue-sync cycle.

Missing coverage for allow-other-integration and deassign blocking

In tests/sentry/models/test_groupassignee.py the only cycle test is test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration which asserts outbound is suppressed when source equals target. There is no test that a different source integration still syncs outward, nor that deassign with a matching AssignmentSource is suppressed. Consequence: a regression that over-suppresses all outbound sync or that leaves the deassign loop unfixed would not be caught.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.

false_positives.candidate:
Partition lock creation is racy

In src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py OffsetTracker._get_partition_lock does get then setdefault on partition_locks dict with no global lock. Two threads for the same new Partition can both miss the get and create different Lock objects, so add_offset/complete_offset/get_committable_offsets for that partition can run under different locks. Consequence is corrupted all_offsets/outstanding sets and wrong committable offsets, causing duplicate processing or skipping offsets.

Commit scan loops over offset gaps

In src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets iterates range(start, max_offset+1) to find contiguous completion. If offsets are sparse (e.g. 100 and 1_000_100 after a gap, filtering, or different assignment), it loops ~1M times per partition on every 1s commit tick. Consequence is CPU burn and stalled commit thread, delaying all commits.

Failed work is still marked complete and committed

In src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py OrderedQueueWorker.run catches all Exceptions from result_processor, logs, then unconditionally calls offset_tracker.complete_offset in finally. The class docstring claims only successful processing is committed. Consequence is a poison or transient failure advances the committed offset past the failed message, so the message is lost with no retry or DLQ.

Unbounded queues provide no backpressure

In src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() with no maxsize while claiming natural backpressure. If a queue's worker stalls on a slow subscription, submit keeps appending via non-blocking put. Consequence is unbounded memory growth and OOM, instead of blocking the Arroyo poll loop.

Shutdown abandons queued work

In src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown=True before draining, and OrderedQueueWorker.run exits when that flag is set after the current item. Remaining queued WorkItems are never processed and their offsets never completed. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close calls this path, so normal close/rebalance drops in-memory work and forces redelivery or stalls commits.

Shared queue pool is shut down by per-partition strategy

In src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/result_consumer.py create_thread_queue_parallel_worker shares factory.queue_pool across all strategies from create_with_partitions, but SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close/terminate calls queue_pool.shutdown. Closing one partition assignment (e.g. on rebalance) kills workers for all current and future assignments reusing the factory pool, after which submit either blocks or raises queue.ShutDown and messages stop being processed.

join ignores timeout and always closes

In src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(timeout) ignores the timeout argument and unconditionally calls close, which joins the commit thread for 5s and shuts down the pool. Callers expecting Arroyo join semantics (wait up to timeout without destroying the strategy) instead get a destructive shutdown.

wait_until_empty ignores in-flight work

In src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty and get_stats use only Queue.qsize. An item taken by a worker but not yet finished or offset-completed leaves qsize at 0. Consequence is callers conclude processing is done while work is still in flight, causing premature commits checks and flaky tests.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

OptimizedCursorPaginator allows negative-offset DB slicing

Django QuerySets do not support negative slicing and raise AssertionError, so a crafted cursor string like "0:-5:0" causes a 500/DoS. true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same code: in OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features is true and cursor.offset < 0, the negative cursor.offset is passed as start_offset for queryset slicing. This is the same underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BasePaginator now passes negative offset for prev cursors

BasePaginator.get_result was changed from queryset[offset:stop] to start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset. For is_prev cursors the offset is used unclamped, so a client-supplied cursor with negative offset and is_prev=1 still reaches queryset[negative:stop]. true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: in BasePaginator.get_result, when cursor.is_prev is true, the offset is used without clamping, so a negative value can reach queryset slicing.

false_positives.candidate:
Hidden optimized_pagination flag switches to vulnerable paginator

The endpoint adds an undocumented ?optimized_pagination=true query param that, for any superuser or member with has_global_access, switches from DateTimePaginator to OptimizedCursorPaginator with enable_advanced_features=True. This exposes the negative-offset path to a broad set of users on a sensitive audit-log endpoint with no tests or validation, widening attack surface unrelated to the spans-buffer title.

Mandatory end_timestamp_precise lookup crashes consumer on missing field

process_batch now does val["end_timestamp_precise"] with direct dict access. Any span event missing that field raises KeyError inside the Arroyo batch, failing the whole batch, blocking commits and causing consumer crash-loop/backlog instead of skipping or defaulting. Previously Span did not require the field.

ZUNIONSTORE without AGGREGATE MAX corrupts scores on duplicates

The migration from SUNIONSTORE to ZUNIONSTORE uses default SUM aggregation. If the same payload member exists in both source sets (retry, duplicate ingest, overlapping parent/span buffers), its score (end_timestamp_precise) is summed to 2x timestamp, corrupting ordering and future ZPOPMIN eviction victims. Should use AGGREGATE MAX.

max_segment_spans enforcement removed, truncation is silent

_load_segment_data no longer checks max_segment_spans, drops the segment_span_count_exceeded metric and error log, and leaves max_segment_spans config unused. Oversized segments are now silently truncated to 1000 in Lua via ZPOPMIN (hardcoded, off-by-one vs 1001 default) and flushed as incomplete instead of being skipped/logged, causing silent span loss.

Redirect traversal cut from 10000 to 1000 fragments deep traces

The redirect-following loop was reduced from 10000 to 1000 iterations. Traces/segment trees deeper than 1000 will stop early with an unresolved set_span_id, so spans that should merge into one segment stay in separate Redis keys and flush as fragmented segments. This is a correctness regression for deep traces to save Lua time.

false_negatives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unstable hash() cache key with 60s stale allowlist returns wrong counts

In src/sentry/api/helpers/error_upsampling.py the cache key is built with Python hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids))). Python hash() is salted per-process, so different workers produce different keys and never share cache, and collisions are possible. Worse, the cached value is only allowlist eligibility cached for 60 seconds. If the allowlist changes, queries for up to 60s use the stale decision and return upsampled sum(sample_weight) instead of count() or vice versa. invalidate_upsampling_cache is defined but never called anywhere, so there is no invalidation. The new endpoint tests reuse the same org and project ids with different mocked allowlists, so the second test will hit the first test's cached True and get wrong results.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate points out that the cache key is built with Python's hash(), which is salted per process. As a result, workers produce different keys and don't share cache. This is the same core issue as the golden comment. The candidate also mentions invalidation problems.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling check uses outer dataset and request instead of scoped query

In src/sentry/api/endpoints/organization_events_stats.py _get_event_stats receives scoped_dataset and query as arguments but calls is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request) using the outer closure dataset and the original request. The dashboard-split factory calls the same function with split_dataset=discover and rewritten queries like (query) AND !event.type:transaction. Because the check ignores scoped_dataset and the query argument and instead inspects request.GET, split queries are evaluated against the wrong dataset and wrong query string, so errors routed to discover will not be upsampled and transactions routed elsewhere may be.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say the upsampling check is given the outer dataset when it should use scoped_dataset. As a result, dashboard split queries routed to discover skip upsampling. The candidate also flags the query/request issue, but its core point is the same as the golden comment.

false_positives.candidate:
Error detection only matches event.type:error substring

In src/sentry/api/helpers/error_upsampling.py _is_error_focused_query returns True only if the lowercased request query string contains event.type:error. Dayjs objects compared with === never equal

In checkIfIsAvailable the code tests `dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...)` to detect a zero-length date override (day marked unavailable). `dayjs()` returns an object, so `===` compares object identity and is always false. As a result a full-day block is never detected, `dateOverrideExist` stays true and the function later returns true (available). true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same bug: dayjs objects are compared with ===, which checks object identity, so the comparison is always false. The candidate adds what this breaks downstream, but the underlying problem is identical.

false_positives.candidate:
Working-hours check fails with split hours

In checkIfIsAvailable availability is rejected if `workingHours.find(workingHour => slot is outside that workingHour)` finds any entry. If a user has two intervals on the same weekday (e.g. morning and afternoon), a slot inside one interval is outside the other, so `find` always succeeds and every slot is marked unavailable. The correct test is that a slot is available if it is inside any interval, not that it is outside any interval. Fixed hosts with split hours will show no slots.

Date-override containment misses slots overflowing the override

In checkIfIsAvailable a slot is deemed outside a date override only if `slotEnd <= overrideStart` or `slotStart > overrideEnd`. A slot that starts inside the override but ends after `override.end` (e.g. override 10:00-11:00, slot 10:30-11:30) satisfies neither condition, so `find` returns undefined and the slot is treated as inside the override and returned as available. This allows bookings that extend beyond the override window. The same block also uses `isAfter` instead of same-or-after for the end boundary, so a slot starting exactly at override end is treated as inside.

Timezone offset computed from Date.toString()

In getSlots the offsets are computed as `dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone)` and `.tz(timeZone)`. `Date.toString()` produces a locale-dependent string without explicit offset that dayjs must re-parse, which can lose the original instant, depend on server locale, and give the wrong `utcOffset()` around DST. The Date object should be passed directly to dayjs, e.g. `dayjs(override.start).tz(...)`, to preserve the instant.

Date-override timezone shift drops day rollover

In getSlots an override is converted to invitee minutes-since-midnight via `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset).hour()*60+minute`. Only hour/minute are kept and the result is applied to the original `startOfInviteeDay`. If the invitee-organizer offset moves the override across midnight, the portion belonging to the adjacent invitee day is still placed on the original day (or `start >= end` and skipped entirely). This creates slots on the wrong day or drops availability for timezones far apart.

Deleting a public service method in the same change that converts internals to raw SQL is a breaking contract change and requires updating all call sites in the same PR.

toEqual on Prisma.Sql compares template segmentation, not SQL semantics

The test at packages/lib/server/service/__tests__/insightsBooking.integration-test.ts:295 expects team/org/combined conditions with expect(conditions).toEqual(Prisma.sql`...flat template...`). The service builds the same SQL text via nested interpolation, e.g. Prisma.sql`(${acc}) OR (${condition})` and Prisma.sql`(${acc}) AND (${condition})` in buildOrgAuthorizationCondition, buildTeamAuthorizationCondition and buildFilterConditions. Prisma.Sql stores strings[] plus values[]; nested Sql values are flattened by splicing, so the resulting strings[] segmentation differs from a hand-written flat template even when the final SQL text and bound values are identical. toEqual therefore fails on false negatives, making the authorization/filter tests red while the query is semantically correct.
